title: Dover Beach
description: Probably written in 1851 on the honeymoon at Dover and published in the New Poems of 1867: the most famous short poem of Victorian doubt, spoken by a lover to his beloved at the window of a house on the strait.
plot_or_argument: The speaker describes the calm sea, the cliffs and the moonlit strait, and hears in the tide the 'eternal note of sadness'; he recalls Sophocles hearing the same note on the Aegean, and the poem turns to the 'Sea of Faith' that was once full and is now retreating, leaving the world a 'darkling plain' of ignorant armies clashing by night.
historical_context: The 1851 honeymoon, the geological and biblical criticism of the 1850s-60s, and the publication of the poem at a moment (1867) when the doubt it articulates had become a public controversy after Essays and Reviews (1860) and the Colenso affair.
literary_significance: 'Dover Beach' is the most quoted Victorian poem and the definitive lyric of the retreat of faith; its 'darkling plain' and 'ignorant armies' have become permanent English images, and the poem's structure of a private love scene carrying a public argument is the model for the modern meditative lyric.

title: Culture and Anarchy: An Essay in Political and Social Criticism
description: The founding text of English cultural criticism, first published as a series of essays in the Cornhill Magazine in 1867-68 and collected in 1869: an argument that the state must promote 'culture' — the best that has been thought and said — against the anarchy of class interest and the 'machinery' of Victorian liberalism.
plot_or_argument: The argument proceeds by a survey of English society as three classes — the Barbarians (aristocracy), the Philistines (middle class) and the Populace (working class) — each of which Arnold finds wanting in 'sweetness and light'; the remedy is the cultivation of the 'best self' through education and the action of the state, which Arnold calls 'the organ of our collective best self'.
historical_context: The 1867 Reform Act and the Hyde Park riots, the campaign for national education, the disestablishment of the Irish Church, and the Victorian debate between Nonconformist voluntarism and state action.
literary_significance: Culture and Anarchy gave English criticism its vocabulary and its central problem: the relation of culture to democracy. 'Philistine', 'Barbarian', 'sweetness and light' and 'culture' as Arnold defines it all derive from this book, and its argument shaped the English debate on education and the state from Huxley and Spencer to the Newbolt Report and the founding of English studies.

title: Essays in Criticism
description: The first series of 1865 collects the essays that established Arnold as the leading critic of the age — 'The Function of Criticism at the Present Time', 'The Literary Influence of Academies', 'Maurice de Guérin', 'Eugénie de Guérin', 'Heine', 'Joubert', 'Spinoza and the Bible', 'Marcus Aurelius' — and the second series of 1888 adds the essays on Wordsworth, Byron, Shelley, Gray, Keats and Tolstoy.
plot_or_argument: The central argument, stated in 'The Function of Criticism', is that criticism must be disinterested: it must 'learn and propagate the best that is known and thought in the world' and must resist the practical, party and personal considerations that make English criticism provincial. The essays on French and German writers are examples of that disinterestedness applied to English culture.
historical_context: The 1860s: the periodical culture of the Cornhill and the Fortnightly, the Victorian ignorance of continental literature, and the crisis of religious belief that Arnold addressed in the same years.
literary_significance: Essays in Criticism is the founding work of modern English criticism: its definition of criticism as disinterested and its demand that English culture learn from the continent set the terms for the discipline into which English studies later grew, and its second series shaped the Victorian and modern estimate of the Romantic poets.

title: Literature and Dogma: An Essay towards a Better Apprehension of the Bible
description: Published in 1873 and the central work of Arnold's later religious criticism: an attempt to save the Bible and the Christian moral tradition from both the dogmatic theologians and the scientific sceptics by treating the biblical language as 'literature' and 'poetry' rather than as metaphysics.
plot_or_argument: Arnold argues that the word 'God' in the Bible is used as a term of 'the Eternal, not ourselves, that makes for righteousness', not as the name of a metaphysical person; the book examines the language of the Bible, the meaning of miracles and prophecy, and the 'Aberglaube' (extra-belief) that has overlaid the original 'verifiable' experience of righteousness.
historical_context: Darwin's Origin (1859) and Descent (1871), Essays and Reviews (1860), the Colenso controversy and the new biblical criticism, and the Victorian debate on the disestablishment of the Irish Church (1869).
literary_significance: Literature and Dogma is the classic Victorian attempt to preserve religious experience after the collapse of dogmatic belief, and it invented the modern idea of the Bible as literature; its influence on Pater, on the modernist theology of the twentieth century and on the study of the Bible in English departments has been continuous.

title: On the Study of Celtic Literature
description: Four lectures delivered as Professor of Poetry at Oxford in 1865-66 and published in 1867: the founding English study of Celtic literature, and the text in which Arnold set out his influential and contested theory of the Celtic 'genius'.
plot_or_argument: Arnold surveys the Welsh, Irish and Gaelic literary remains, argues that English literature owes to Celtic a quality of 'natural magic' and sentiment which it needs, and calls for the study of Celtic at Oxford; the argument is conducted with Arnold's characteristic mixture of sympathy and condescension toward the 'Celtic race'.
historical_context: The 1860s Celtic revival, the Welsh Sunday Closing agitation and the Irish land question, and the new philology of the 1860s.
literary_significance: On the Study of Celtic Literature founded the academic study of Celtic literature in English and introduced the 'Celtic note' into English criticism; it is also a central text for the modern critique of nineteenth-century racial thinking, and it gave the Irish and Welsh revivals of the 1890s their critical vocabulary.

title: The Wreck of the Deutschland
description: Written in 1875-76 on the wreck of the Deutschland, which sank in the Thames estuary in December 1875 with five Franciscan nuns among the drowned; offered to the Month and refused, and unpublished until the 1918 edition: the first poem in sprung rhythm.
plot_or_argument: The ode opens with the poet's personal address to God, turns to the shipwreck and to the tall nun's cry 'Christ, King, Head', and ends in a prayer for the conversion of England; the wreck is read as an instance of divine mastery and of the 'harvest' of the tall nun's faith.
historical_context: The Deutschland disaster of 7 December 1875, the Jesuit province of North Wales where Hopkins was studying, the conversion of England for which the Jesuits prayed, and the Oxford Movement's legacy.
literary_significance: The Wreck of the Deutschland is the greatest English religious ode of the century and the work in which sprung rhythm was invented; its rejection by the Month kept Hopkins's poetry unpublished in his lifetime and its publication in 1918 changed the technique of English verse.

title: The Windhover: To Christ Our Lord
description: Written on 30 May 1877, the day after his ordination, and the most famous of Hopkins's sonnets: the kestrel's flight read as an image of Christ's mastery and of the beauty that 'buckles' the self.
plot_or_argument: The octave watches the kestrel hovering and describes its mastery in compound epithets; the sestet turns from the bird to Christ and to the paradox that the 'sheer plod' of ordinary labour and the 'blue-bleak embers' of a dying fire are more beautiful than the bird's brilliance, because they 'fall, gall themselves, and gash gold-vermilion'.
historical_context: The 1877 ordination, the Welsh landscape of St Beuno's, and the Ignatian meditation on created things as the 'footprints' of God.
literary_significance: 'The Windhover' is the most anthologised Victorian sonnet after 'God's Grandeur' and the technical showpiece of sprung rhythm; it is the central English poem of the sacramental imagination, and its critical history (from Bridges's puzzlement to the modern readings of Empson and others) is a case study in the reception of difficulty.

title: God's Grandeur
description: Written in 1877: a sonnet on the grandeur of God in the world and the human refusal to see it — 'the world is charged with the grandeur of God' — and one of the founding texts of modern nature poetry.
plot_or_argument: The octave states the presence of God's grandeur in the world and the way 'generations have trod, have trod, have trod' until the ground is seared; the sestet turns to the renewal of the world by the Holy Ghost, whose brooding over the bent world makes it 'warm with the grandeur of God' again.
historical_context: The industrial England of the 1870s, the Jesuit training in Lancashire and Wales, and the 1877 sermons on the created world as the manifestation of God.
literary_significance: 'God's Grandeur' is the most quoted Victorian religious sonnet and the central poem of Hopkins's sacramental nature poetry; its combination of industrial imagery with the doctrine of the Holy Ghost has made it a permanent text for the criticism of Victorian religion and of modern ecology.

title: The Terrible Sonnets
description: The 'terrible' or 'sonnets of desolation' written in Dublin in 1885-88 — 'Carrion Comfort', 'No worst, there is none', 'To seem the stranger lies my lot', 'I wake and feel the fell of dark, not day', 'Patience, hard thing!', 'My own heart let me more have pity on' — and the most powerful English poems of spiritual desolation.
plot_or_argument: The sonnets record the loss of consolation in prayer: the soul wrestles with a God who seems to withhold grace, the mind is reduced to 'the mind's own self-taste', and the sequence ends in the effort to accept the will of God without the feeling of his presence.
historical_context: Hopkins's Dublin years as Professor of Greek at the Royal University, his isolation in Ireland, his failing health and his conflict with the political and religious atmosphere of the country, and the spiritual theology of the dark night.
literary_significance: The terrible sonnets are the central documents of Victorian religious suffering and the greatest devotional poems in English of the nineteenth century; their analysis of depression has made them permanent texts of the modern literature of mental illness, and their influence on the twentieth-century religious lyric is direct.

title: Binsey Poplars
description: Written in March 1879 after the felling of the poplar trees along the Isis at Binsey, near Oxford: the most quoted English poem of ecological mourning and one of the clearest statements of Hopkins's doctrine of inscape.
plot_or_argument: The poem records the felling of the aspens 'that dandled a sandalled shadow', laments that the 'sweet especial rural scene' can never be restored, and ends with the warning that 'ten or twelve' strokes of the axe 'unselve' the countryside.
historical_context: The felling of the Binsey poplars in 1879 and the Victorian destruction of rural landscape by industry and agriculture, which Hopkins addressed in several poems and letters.
literary_significance: 'Binsey Poplars' is the founding poem of English ecological literature and the key text for Hopkins's theory of inscape as the individual signature of a place; its coinage 'unselve' has become a permanent English word for environmental destruction.

title: Goblin Market and Other Poems
description: Published in 1862 with illustrations by Dante Gabriel Rossetti, and the volume that made her reputation: Goblin Market, 'Remember', 'A Birthday', 'After Death', 'The Convent Threshold', 'Up-Hill' and 'An Apple Gathering'.
plot_or_argument: In Goblin Market, Laura buys and eats the goblins' fruit and begins to waste away, calling for 'more'; her sister Lizzie resists the merchants' assault and returns with the juice of the fruit on her face, which restores Laura; the poem ends with the two as wives and mothers telling the story to their children.
literary_form: Poetry collection; title poem in irregular rhymed couplets
historical_context: The 1860s, the Pre-Raphaelite circle and its treatment of the fallen woman, the Victorian debate on sensual temptation and the spiritual reading of fairy tale, and the penitentiary work at Highgate where Christina Rossetti taught from 1876.
literary_significance: Goblin Market is the most discussed Victorian poem by a woman and a central text of modern feminist criticism, read as an allegory of consumerism, of sexual knowledge, of sisterhood and of the Eucharist; its fairy tale surface and its theological depth made it the model for the fantastic moral tale from MacDonald and Kingsley to the modern fantasy.

title: The Prince's Progress and Other Poems
description: Published in 1866 with illustrations by her brother: the title poem, a ballad-allegory of the prince who delays on his journey and finds the princess dead, together with 'The Convent Threshold', 'A Royal Princess', 'Under the Rose' and the devotional lyrics.
plot_or_argument: The prince sets out to claim his bride, is delayed by the temptations of the road, and arrives to find her dead; 'A Royal Princess' concerns a princess who gives her wealth to the poor; 'Under the Rose' is a legend of the Virgin's rose.
literary_form: Poetry collection; title poem in ballad stanzas
historical_context: The 1860s Pre-Raphaelite interest in the ballad and the allegory, the Victorian cult of the dead virgin (Elizabeth Siddal died in 1862), and the Anglo-Catholic devotional culture of the period.
literary_significance: The Prince's Progress is the finest Victorian allegorical ballad and the clearest statement of Rossetti's theology of delay and loss; its treatment of the princess's autonomy (as against the prince's dilatoriness) has made it a key text in the modern reading of her gender politics.

title: Sing-Song: A Nursery Rhyme Book
description: Published in 1872 with illustrations by Arthur Hughes: 120 nursery rhymes, riddles, lullabies and poems on natural history written for and about children, and one of the foundation texts of English children's verse.
plot_or_argument: The poems are short lyrics on the moon, the wind, birds, flowers, death and sleep, many of them in question-and-answer form or in dialogue with a child; some are riddles whose answers lie in the natural world.
historical_context: The 1870s and the new market for illustrated children's books (Caldecott, Crane, Greenaway), the Victorian cult of childhood, and the mortality rates among children that the poems accept without evasion.
literary_significance: Sing-Song is one of the purest bodies of children's verse in English and a central document in the history of Victorian children's literature. Its frank treatment of death and its formal perfection have made it a permanent text for the study of the Victorian child, and it influenced de la Mare and the children's poets of the twentieth century.

title: A Pageant and Other Poems
description: Published in 1881, containing 'A Pageant', 'Monna Innominata: A Sonnet of Sonnets', 'The Key-Note' and the devotional and elegiac lyrics of her later manner: the volume in which she turns fully to the preparation for death.
plot_or_argument: 'Monna Innominata' is a sequence of fourteen sonnets in which a woman speaks the unspoken love of the great Tuscan poets, prefaced by an argument that the Lady of the sonnet tradition has never spoken for herself; 'A Pageant' is a series of visionary poems on the months and on mortality.
literary_form: Poetry collection, including the sonnet sequence 'Monna Innominata'
historical_context: The 1880s, her increasing illness (Graves' disease diagnosed in 1871), the devotional life at Highgate, and the aesthetic movement's cult of the sonnet.
literary_significance: A Pageant and Other Poems contains the most formally perfect sonnet sequence of the Victorian period by a woman and the one that most directly challenges the male tradition. Its preface to Monna Innominata is a founding text for the feminist criticism of the sonnet tradition, and the volume's death poems are among the greatest English devotional lyrics.

title: Verses
description: Privately printed in 1893 for the Society of the Sacred Cross and reprinted in 1896 as New Poems: the devotional verse and prose of her last years, including 'The World', 'A Better Resurrection' and the poems on the Eucharist.
plot_or_argument: The poems are devotional lyrics on the sacraments, the saints, the love of God and the preparation for death, with a number of paraphrases and hymns.
historical_context: The 1890s, her final illness and the Anglo-Catholic devotional revival of the period, and the private circulation of devotional literature among religious communities.
literary_significance: Verses is the late devotional testament of the century's finest religious poet, and it shows the continuity of the Tractarian tradition in English poetry at the very end of the period; its recovery in the twentieth century completed the modern edition of Rossetti's work.

title: The Early Italian Poets
description: Published in 1861 as The Early Italian Poets from Ciullo d'Alcamo to Dante Alighieri (1100-1200-1300), and reissued in 1874 as Dante and His Circle: the translations of Dante's Vita Nuova, the poetry of the stilnovisti, and the poems of the contemporary Italian poets, with Rossetti's prefaces.
plot_or_argument: The volume translates the Vita Nuova entire, with its prose narrative of Dante's love for Beatrice, together with poems by Guido Cavalcanti, Cino da Pistoia, Guido Guinicelli and others, and a selection of the poets of Dante's circle.
historical_context: The 1850s-60s revival of Dante (the Pre-Raphaelite paintings, the 1862 centenary, the new editions), the Victorian interest in the Italian Middle Ages, and Rossetti's own Italian inheritance.
literary_significance: The Early Italian Poets is the finest body of verse translation of the Victorian period and the work that established Dante's Vita Nuova as a central English text; it is the foundation of the modern English reception of the dolce stil novo and the model for Pound's and Eliot's use of medieval Italian poetry.

title: Poems
description: Published in 1870 after the exhumation of the manuscript buried with Elizabeth Siddal in 1869: the collection that made Rossetti famous and provoked Robert Buchanan's attack on the 'Fleshly School of Poetry' in the Contemporary Review in October 1871.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains The House of Life (a sonnet sequence on love and death), 'The Blessed Damozel', 'Jenny', 'Sister Helen', 'Troy Town' and the ballads; the sonnets record the love of the speaker for a woman who is at once bodily and spiritual, and the ballads turn the same material into supernatural narrative.
literary_form: Poetry collection, including The House of Life
historical_context: The 1860s-70s, the aesthetic movement's doctrine of art for beauty's sake, the death of Elizabeth Siddal in 1862, and the Buchanan controversy over the morality of the 'fleshly' school.
literary_significance: Poems of 1870 is the central volume of English aesthetic poetry and the work that made 'the fleshly school' a public controversy; The House of Life is the major English sonnet sequence of the century after Barrett Browning's, and Buchanan's attack became the defining document in the Victorian debate about the autonomy of art.

title: Ballads and Sonnets
description: Published in 1881, the year before his death, and containing the completed House of Life in its final order, together with 'The White Ship', 'The King's Tragedy', 'Rose Mary' and the late sonnets.
plot_or_argument: The ballads are supernatural narratives of doom — the loss of the White Ship, the murder of James I of Scotland, the crystal ball of Rose Mary — and the sonnets complete the sequence of love, loss and the memorial image.
historical_context: The 1880s, Rossetti's last years at Kelmscott and Cheyne Walk, his addiction to chloral and his failing sight, and the aesthetic movement at its height.
literary_significance: Ballads and Sonnets is the final form of Rossetti's poetic testament, and The House of Life in its 1881 order is the definitive English sonnet sequence of the aesthetic movement; the volume's influence on Yeats and on the 1890s is direct.

title: The Blessed Damozel
description: Written in 1847, published in the Germ in 1850 and revised for the 1870 Poems: the poem in which the Pre-Raphaelite image of the beloved in heaven was first fully stated, and the text of Rossetti's own painting of 1871-79.
plot_or_argument: The blessed damozel leans out from the bar of heaven and looks down to the earth where her lover still lives; she prays that he may join her, and the poem ends with her tears and with the lover's sense of the distance between them.
historical_context: The 1847-50 Pre-Raphaelite movement, the Dantean model of Beatrice in paradise, and the Victorian poetry of the dead beloved.
literary_significance: The Blessed Damozel is the founding poem of Pre-Raphaelite poetry and the work in which the aesthetic movement's image of the woman in heaven was created; it is the source of the pictorial and poetic tradition that runs through Burne-Jones and the 1890s.

title: Jenny
description: Written in 1848-70 and published in the 1870 Poems: a dramatic monologue spoken by a young man over the sleeping figure of a London prostitute, in which his aesthetic and sentimental reflections are gradually exposed as a failure of moral imagination.
plot_or_argument: The speaker sits with the sleeping Jenny, compares her to his cousin Nell and to the women of society, reflects on her history and on the 'double standard' that condemns her while excusing him, and at last covers her hair and leaves, having reached no decision and no action.
historical_context: The 1848-70 debate on prostitution (the Contagious Diseases Acts of 1864-69), the Victorian 'social evil' literature, and the Pre-Raphaelite fascination with the fallen woman.
literary_significance: 'Jenny' is the most direct Victorian poetic treatment of prostitution and the double standard, and its technique — a speaker whose cultivated sensibility becomes evidence against him — is the most sophisticated use of the dramatic monologue for social criticism in the period. Modern criticism has made it a central text in the study of Victorian gender and sexuality.

title: 'The New Colossus'
description: Written in 1883 for the Bartholdi Pedestal Fund and inscribed on the Statue of Liberty in 1903: the founding poem of American immigration.
plot_or_argument: The sonnet contrasts the Colossus of Rhodes, the giant of antiquity that celebrated conquest, with the American statue that stands at the harbour and cries to the old world to give her the tired, the poor, the huddled masses yearning to breathe free.
historical_context: 1883: the campaign to fund the pedestal of the Statue of Liberty, the mass immigration of the 1880s, and the American debate on the admission of the poor of Europe.
literary_significance: 'The New Colossus' is the most quoted American sonnet and the founding poem of the American immigration tradition: its inscription on the Statue of Liberty in 1903 made it the national statement of the purpose of America, and its lines have been quoted in every debate on immigration since.

title: Songs of a Semite: The Dance to Death and Other Poems
description: Published in 1882 and the first English book of poetry to treat the Jewish people as a modern nation: poems of the persecutions and the Zionist hope.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains 'The Dance to Death', a verse tragedy on the massacre of the Jews of Nordhausen in 1349, together with lyrics on the Russian pogroms of 1881, the Jewish exile, and the hope of a return to Palestine.
historical_context: 1880-82: the Russian pogroms of 1881, the beginning of American Zionism, the Jewish immigration to New York, and the English tradition of the verse tragedy.
literary_significance: Songs of a Semite is the founding text of American Zionist literature and the first English poetry collection to treat Jewish persecution as a contemporary political subject: its verse tragedy on a medieval massacre made it a landmark, and it prepared the way for 'The New Colossus' and for the literature of American Zionism.

title: Admetus and Other Poems
description: Published in 1871 and Lazarus's first mature collection: a verse drama on the Alcestis myth and a series of classical and personal lyrics.
plot_or_argument: The title poem retells the story of Admetus, whose wife Alcestis dies for him, and of Heracles who brings her back from the dead; the other poems treat love, art, death and the classical inheritance in the manner of the English romantic poets.
historical_context: 1871: the American classical revival, the influence of the English poets on American verse, and the New York literary world of the 1870s.
literary_significance: Admetus and Other Poems established Lazarus as one of the most accomplished American poets of her generation: its classical verse drama and its lyrics of love and death showed a mastery of form rare among American women poets, and it was praised by Emerson.

title: The Poems of Emma Lazarus
description: Published posthumously in 1889 and the collected edition that made Lazarus's reputation: the lyrics, the verse dramas and the poems of the Jewish nation.
plot_or_argument: The two volumes gather the whole of her poetry — the early classical lyrics, 'Admetus', 'The Spagnoletto', the Heine translations, 'The Dance to Death', the poems of the pogroms and 'The New Colossus' — with a biographical memoir by her sister.
historical_context: 1889: the year of her death, the American Jewish community of the 1880s, and the posthumous recognition of a poet who had died at thirty-eight.
literary_significance: The Poems of Emma Lazarus is the collected edition that established her as the first American poet of the Jewish people and of immigration: it made 'The New Colossus' available to the campaign that inscribed it on the Statue of Liberty, and it is the essential text of her achievement.

title: 'The Marshes of Glynn'
description: Published in 1878 and the greatest American nature poem of the South: the poet's vision of the Georgia marshes at dawn.
plot_or_argument: The poet goes out among the marshes of Glynn at dawn and feels himself dissolved into the ocean of light and air; the poem moves from the description of the marsh to a vision of the infinite, in which the self is lost and found in the divine unity of the natural world.
historical_context: 1878: the Georgia coast, the post-war South, the transcendentalist inheritance of Emerson and Whitman, and Lanier's own tuberculosis and poverty.
literary_significance: 'The Marshes of Glynn' is the finest American nature poem between Whitman and Frost and the central poem of the Southern landscape: its musical structure and its mystical vision made it a landmark, and it is the poem in which Lanier's theory of verse as music is most completely realized.
